The sun doesn’t “turn the rain on” like a switch. Instead, the rain is just part of nature’s way of keeping our planet healthy. When rain falls, it soaks into the ground, helps plants grow, and keeps the air clean. Sometimes the sky gets too full of those water droplets, and they fall all at once—that’s why it rains so heavily!

Next time you’re inside on a rainy day, you could try drawing a picture of the water cycle, reading a book about clouds, or just listening to the sound of the raindrops on the roof. It’s a good reminder that the world is always working, even when we can’t go outside.

Here's what's going on: Your body has tiny muscles under your skin called **arrector pili muscles** (say: AR-ek-tor PY-ly). When you get cold, these muscles squeeze the tiny hairs on your skin, making bumps. It's like your body is trying to help keep you warm by making your hair stand up.

You might also get goosebumps when you're happy or excited, like when you hear a really cool song or see something amazing. That's because the same muscles get a little twitchy with excitement too.

The bumps usually go away when you warm up. So next time you're waiting for the bus and feel them, just know your body is doing its job to help you stay cozy!
